[09:14:33] growing attachment to her farm, through which flows a small stream known to history as Little Bull Run. But the woman on the land near the Manassas battlefield was not really a farm wife. [09:16:07] The plan was to bring thousands of upscale corporate workers to the area, expanding the county's tax base while blending with the environment. [09:16:47] A citizens group was formed, but could raise only about $5,000 for a legal battle. The loss of Penn Station created an outcry across the country, the effects of which we still feel today. [12:45:52] lose something as important as Penn Station, said Paul Goldberger, architecture critic for New York Magazine. I sometimes think of it as the building that died so that others might live. New York's landmark preservation law was a direct inspiration for the National Historic Preservation Act, which expanded those same protections on historical sites across the United States.

[12:46:18] Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act charges the National Park Service with preserving and protecting America's story. Whenever the National Park Service has a project involving federal land or funding, Section 106 must be done. It also applies to any cultural resources listed on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. The mission is to protect our history by ensuring that no historical structure or landscape will ever again be lost through lack of planning or foresight. While the impact of destroying a historic landmark like

[12:46:54] Penn Station is obvious, many small and often well-intended projects in our parks could have similar unforeseen consequences. Digging a hole for a fence could accidentally cut through an ancient grave. A new comfort station situated in a battlefield could affect the viewshed. A new trail could lead to a sensitive resource such as an archaeological site. The grass you are maintaining never existed historically and could change the landscape. A new road adds shoulders and pullouts that could impact an archaeological resource.

[12:47:28] Painting a historic building in new color or adding modern windows may change the historic character. The Section 106 compliance process helps us find solutions to balance the goals of historic preservation and park priorities and must be followed for every project.

[12:47:44] It is for improvements as well as demolitions, for routine maintenance and upkeep, as well as new construction, for small projects as well as for big ones. Section 106 matters because our history matters. It protects structures like Penn Station from ever being lost again without first ensuring careful and thoughtful study.

[12:48:04] Following the 106 process represents the respect we have for our resources and the guarantee that they will be protected for future generations.
